title: Quorum Systems
summary: Tuning consistency vs availability with N/W/R quorums, sloppy quorums, and hinted handoff.

slides.markdown:
[Leaderless replication](replication-strategies) writes to several replicas and reads from several replicas — but how many of each, out of how many total, before you trust the result? **Quorums** answer that with three numbers: N (total replicas), W (replicas that must ack a write), R (replicas queried on a read).

Get W and R right relative to N and you can guarantee a read always sees the latest write, without ever needing a leader. This topic is the actual math behind "leaderless doesn't mean inconsistent" — and where it quietly breaks.

slides.sectionTitle: Quorums: reads and writes that overlap by design
slides.markdown:
A **quorum** is simply "more than half" (or some chosen threshold) of a group agreeing before an operation counts as done. In leaderless replication, a write is considered successful once **W** replicas acknowledge it, and a read is considered done once **R** replicas have responded (with the client reconciling their answers, usually by picking the newest timestamped value).

The trick is choosing W and R so that any write quorum and any read quorum are guaranteed to share at least one replica — that shared replica is what guarantees a read can see the latest write, even without a leader coordinating anything.

slides.sectionTitle: The N/W/R formula and what W+R>N buys you
slides.markdown:
With **N** total replicas, **W** the write quorum size, and **R** the read quorum size, the rule is: if `W + R > N`, every read quorum and every write quorum must overlap by at least one replica — by the pigeonhole principle, you can't pick W+R replicas out of only N without reusing at least one.

Example: N=3, W=2, R=2 gives W+R=4 > 3, so overlap is guaranteed — any 2-of-3 write and any 2-of-3 read share a replica. That shared replica holds the newest write, so the read is guaranteed to see it (once the client picks the most recent value among the R responses).

This is what lets a leaderless system claim strong-ish consistency without ever electing a leader.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a quorum write and read overlapping across N replicas
slides.markdown:
![Write set and read set of three replicas overlapping at replica 2 under W+R>N](assets/quorum-overlap.svg)

The picture makes the guarantee concrete: the write touched replicas 1 and 2, the read queried replicas 2 and 3 — and replica 2, the overlap, is guaranteed to hold the write. No matter which W replicas a write hits or which R replicas a read hits, with W+R>N there's always at least one node in both sets.

slides.sectionTitle: Tuning consistency vs availability by choosing W and R
slides.markdown:
W and R aren't fixed by the database — they're a tuning knob you set per use case. A **high W** (closer to N) makes writes more durable but slower, and less available if nodes are down. A **high R** makes reads more likely to see the latest data but slower for the same reason. Push both low (W=1, R=1) and you get the fastest, most available system — with the weakest consistency guarantee, since W+R>N no longer holds.

A common real split: write-heavy workloads favor a low W and higher R (fast writes, reads do the work of finding the latest value); read-heavy workloads favor the reverse. Cassandra exposes exactly this as a per-query consistency level (`ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`).

A **strict quorum** requires W or R to be satisfied by the *specific* replicas assigned to that data. If enough of them are unreachable (a network partition, a node down), a strict quorum write simply fails — even if other, healthy nodes exist.

A **sloppy quorum** relaxes this: if the assigned replicas aren't reachable, the write is temporarily accepted by *any* W available nodes instead, trading correctness of placement for availability. Those temporary nodes hold a **hint** — "this belongs to node X" — and once node X recovers, **hinted handoff** forwards the data to its rightful home and the temporary copy is removed.

This is how Dynamo-style stores keep accepting writes during a partition, at the cost of a window where reads might not find the data if they query only the "correct" replicas.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: strict quorum vs sloppy quorum
slides.markdown:
| | Strict quorum | Sloppy quorum |
|---|---|---|
| Which nodes count toward W/R | Only the data's assigned replicas | Any reachable node, temporarily |
| Behavior during a partition | Write fails if assigned replicas are unreachable | Write succeeds via a temporary node holding a hint |
| Consistency guarantee | W+R>N overlap holds as designed | Weaker — a read of assigned replicas may miss a hinted write until handoff completes |
| Availability | Lower under partition | Higher — keeps accepting writes |

**How to decide:** sloppy quorums trade a temporary consistency gap for write availability during failures — worth it for workloads where an unavailable write is worse than a briefly-stale read (Dynamo's original use case: a shopping cart must always accept an add).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: choosing W=1, R=1 and assuming you still have strong consistency
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We're using a quorum-based store, so we're consistent no matter what W and R we pick."

**Why it's wrong:** the consistency guarantee only holds when `W + R > N`. With N=3, setting W=1 and R=1 gives W+R=2, which is *not* greater than 3 — there's no guaranteed overlap, so a read can easily miss the latest write and return stale data. The word "quorum" in the store's name doesn't enforce this for you; the numbers you pick do.

**Correct model:** treat W and R as an explicit trade-off you calculate, not a default that comes free with a Dynamo-style database. If you want strong-ish read consistency, verify W+R>N for the N you're actually running with — and remember sloppy quorums can violate the guarantee anyway during a partition, hints notwithstanding.
